hook.line: Sometimes you need to promise someone you'll stand firm, or tell them you will not be talked out of something. One repeated verb does it.
hook.es: Pase lo que pase, te apoyo.

examples.es: Pase lo que pase, te apoyo.
Digan lo que digan, voy a ir.
Cueste lo que cueste, vamos a defender el café.
examples.en: Whatever it costs, we're going to defend the café.

examples.es: Hagan lo que hagan, el café se queda.
examples.en: Whatever they do, the café stays.
One way or another, we're talking today.

examples.es: Quieras o no, tenemos que hablar.
examples.en: Whether you like it or not, we have to talk. (to a friend)

rule:
Say a verb, then *lo que*, then the same verb again, and you get "whatever": *pase lo que pase*, *digan lo que digan*.

Both verbs take the wish form (*pase*, not *pasa*), and they must be the same verb. You can't swap in a synonym for the second one.

It works with other little words too: *donde* (wherever), *como* (however). Some are set phrases you can learn whole: *cueste lo que cueste*, *sea como sea*, *quieras o no*.

Use it for what will not change: *Pase lo que pase*, I'm here.
smallPrint: Teachers call this a concessive clause: the wish form, repeated, says 'no matter what'. The repeated verb is part of the pattern.

readAndPick.es: Pase lo que pase, te apoyo.
options: Whatever happens, I'm behind you.
If something happens, I'll back you later.
What happened, I backed you.

readAndPick.es: Digan lo que digan, voy a ir.
options: Whatever he says, I'm going.
They said so, so I'm going.
Whatever they say, I'm going.

readAndPick.es: Diga lo que diga Altamira, no vendo.
options: Altamira said so, so I'm not selling.
Whatever Altamira says, I'm not selling.
Altamira says nothing, so I'm not selling.

readAndPick.es: Cueste lo que cueste, vamos a defender el café.
options: Whatever it costs, we're going to defend the café.
It cost a lot, so we defended the café.
If it costs nothing, we'll defend the café.
Even if it's a lot, we talked today.
One way or another, we're talking today.
However it was, we talked today.

readAndPick.es: Quieras o no, tenemos que hablar.
options: If you want, we have to talk. (to a friend)
You wanted to, so we have to talk. (to a friend)
Whether you like it or not, we have to talk. (to a friend)

readAndPick.es: Hagan lo que hagan, el café se queda.
options: Whatever they did, the café stayed.
Whatever they do, the café stays.
They do nothing, so the café stays.

readAndPick.es: Pase lo que pase, no voy a ceder.
options: Whatever happens, I'm not going to give in.
Nothing happened, so I'm not giving in.
If something happens, I'll give in.
Whatever happens, I'm behind you.
What happened, happened.
Whatever happens, happens.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *pase* or *pasa* and type the whole sentence: *Pase lo que ___, te apoyo.*
yourTurn.answer: Pase lo que pase, te apoyo.
yourTurn.why: The second verb copies the first and also takes the wish form: *pase*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: Whatever they say, I'm going.
yourTurn.answer: Digan lo que digan, voy a ir.
yourTurn.why: *Digan* twice, because *ellos* both times and the same verb.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: Whatever it costs, we're going to defend the café.
yourTurn.answer: Cueste lo que cueste, vamos a defender el café.
yourTurn.why: A set phrase: *cueste lo que cueste* repeats *costar* in the wish form.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: Whatever happens, I'm not going to give in.
yourTurn.answer: Pase lo que pase, no voy a ceder.
yourTurn.why: The repeated pair opens the sentence; the real promise follows after the comma.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: Whatever happens, let me know. (to a friend)
yourTurn.why: A command works fine after *pase lo que pase*, with *-me* tacked on the end.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it one speaker: *Digan lo que digan, voy a ir.* Say: Whatever Altamira says, I'm not selling.
yourTurn.answer: Diga lo que diga Altamira, no vendo.
accept: Diga lo que diga Altamira, yo no vendo.
yourTurn.why: One person now, so *diga* twice instead of *digan*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: Whether you like it or not, we have to talk. (to a friend)
yourTurn.answer: Quieras o no, tenemos que hablar.
yourTurn.why: *Quieras o no* is a ready-made phrase for 'like it or not'.

pitfalls.wrong: Pasa lo que pasa, te apoyo.
pitfalls.right: Pase lo que pase, te apoyo.
pitfalls.why: Almost. Plain *pasa* describes what actually happens; the 'whatever' feeling needs the wish form, *pase*.

pitfalls.wrong: Pase lo que ocurra, te apoyo.
pitfalls.right: Pase lo que pase, te apoyo.
pitfalls.why: Say the same verb twice; swapping in a synonym breaks the pattern.

pitfalls.right: Pase lo que pase, te apoyo.
pitfalls.why: English starts with "whatever", but Spanish needs the verb first and again at the end: *pase lo que pase*.

personal: Finish the line with something true about you: *Pase lo que pase, ...* For example, *Pase lo que pase, voy a seguir con mi español.*
